translationRepairs: All under heaven was in turmoil; the Grand Commandant obtaining him was like gaining an enemy state."
All under heaven was in turmoil; for the Grand General to obtain him was like gaining an enemy state.

Focus unit has 大將軍, not 太尉; the prior literal wrongly borrows Grand Commandant from s0043. The proposal fixes the title but still ends with an extraneous closing quote absent from this narrator sentence.

The hundred offices and responsible officials uphold the law and receive orders, thereby cultivating their duties; for dereliction of duty there is execution, for encroaching on another's office there is punishment."

The hundred offices and responsible officials uphold the law and receive orders, thereby cultivating their duties; for dereliction of duty there is execution, for encroaching on another's office there is punishment.
s0004 is narrator prose with no quotation marks in Chinese; the trailing closing quote after 罰 is extraneous, and removing it restores a faithful literal.
Those seated were in the hundreds; all left their mats and prostrated themselves—only Hu alone sat square facing east, addressing Yi by his courtesy name: "How goes the young lord's eminence!"

Hundreds were seated there. All left their mats and prostrated themselves, but Hu alone remained sitting upright, facing east, and addressed Yi familiarly: "How does the young lord enjoy his eminence?"
字謂邑曰 marks familiar address to Yi; 邑 is his given name (商子邑), and the spoken form is 公子, so 'by his courtesy name' is wrong and 'by name' still overstates the naming form used in the quote.
Halfway to a banquet he heard an old woman he knew lay dying of fever in the lane.

Someone once invited Yuan She to a banquet. As he entered the ward gate, a guest told him that the mother of a family he knew was ill and had moved to a house within the ward in hopes of escaping the sickness.

The prior idiomatic invents halfway progress, an old woman, dying of fever, and a lane setting. The worker identified the problem, but its phrase 'a mother known to Yuan She' was unclear; the context is a family he knew whose mother was ill.
Wang Yougong, a county clerk who hated Yuan She, warned Yin, "Humiliate him now and when a real prefect arrives you will crawl back as a clerk while his nameless killers haunt you.

Yuan She had befriended Qi Taibo, a wealthy man of Xinfeng. Taibo's younger maternal half brother, Wang Yougong, had always resented Yuan She and was then a clerk in the county office. He told Yin, "As acting magistrate, you have humiliated Yuan She. Once the permanent magistrate arrives, you will return alone by cart to your old post as a commandery clerk. Yuan She's assassins are as numerous as clouds, and when they kill, no one ever knows who ordered it. The thought should chill you.

The prior idiomatic drops the friendship with Qi Taibo, Wang Yougong's relationship to him, and most of the warning. The worker restored those facts, but its proposed English was overly literal. Parallel editions also confirm that the corrupt local graph 寫 should be 與.
Rebel chiefs who knew his name hunted him down to pay homage.
The rebel chiefs had long heard Yuan She's name and vied to learn where Prefect Yuan was so they could pay their respects to him.
Chinese 爭問原尹何在 explicitly has the rebels asking where Prefect Yuan was. The worker restored the omitted search, but 'paid court' was too formal and potentially misleading here.
Yuan She bolted; Shentu Jian, shamed and furious, announced, "I meant to hold the capital with Yuan Juxian—I would not trade him for one clerk!"

Yuan She planned to flee. Shentu Jian, inwardly resentful and ashamed, put on a show of saying, "I intend to guard the Three Adjuncts together with Yuan Juxian. How could I trade him for a single clerk?"
涉欲亡去 is an intention to flee, 陽言 marks a public pretense, and 共鎮三輔 refers to guarding the Three Adjuncts. The worker found all three errors, but its proposed syntax was wooden.

Then came the famous lords of the blood—Xinling in Wei, Pingyuan in Zhao, Mengchang in Qi, Chunshen in Chu—who traded on royal connections, bankrolled knights-errant, and honored even petty schemers as honored guests.

Then came the famous lords of the blood: Xinling in Wei, Pingyuan in Zhao, Mengchang in Qi, and Chunshen in Chu. Trading on royal connections, they competed in knight-errantry and received even men of the pettiest talents as honored guests.
The proposal correctly restores the Four Lords as the practitioners of knight-errantry, but its cock-crow dog-thieves wording is too literal for the idiomatic line.
Unless an enlightened king is above, surveying them with likes and dislikes, aligning them with ritual and law, how can the people know prohibition and return to rectitude!"
Unless an enlightened king is above, surveying them with likes and dislikes, aligning them with ritual and law, how can the people know prohibition and return to rectitude!
The Chinese is narrator prose after Zengzi's completed quotation, so the unmatched closing quotation mark must be removed.
In an empire in turmoil, securing Ju Meng was like gaining an enemy state.
Amid the empire's turmoil, the Grand General's gaining Ju Meng was reckoned equivalent to securing the allegiance of an entire rival state.
The proposal correctly restores the Grand General as grammatical subject, but the revised wording makes the comparison intelligible in English.

As for such as the Yao clan of the northern road, the various Du of the western road, Qiu Jing of the southern road, Prince Yu of Zhao Tuo of the eastern road, Zhao Diao of Nanyang and their sort—mere Robber Zhis dwelling among the people—how are they worth speaking of!

As for the Yao clan of the northern road, the various Du of the western road, Qiu Jing of the southern road, Zhao Tuoyu, courtesy Gongzi, of the eastern road, Zhao Diao of Nanyang, and their sort, they were mere Robber Zhis living among the people. How are they worth speaking of?
The proposal correctly rejects the false princely title. The received commentarial reading treats Zhao as the surname, Tuoyu as the given name, and Gongzi as the courtesy name.
Yang Jizhu's son, a county clerk, blocked the convoy, so Guo Xie's nephew took the man's head.
Yang Jizhu's son, a county clerk, blocked the convoy, so Guo Xie's elder brother's son took the man's head.
The source explicitly identifies the killer as Guo Xie's elder brother's son, a distinction useful to the family data.

Still, men like Fan Zhongzi in Chang'an, Zhao Wangsun in Huaili, Gao Gongzi in Changling, Guo Wengzhong west of the river, Lu Wengru in Taiyuan, Er Changqing in Linhuai, and Chen Junru in Dongyang wore the knight's label yet behaved with courteous restraint.

Still, men like Fan Zhongzi in Chang'an, Zhao Wangsun in Huaili, Gao Gongzi in Changling, Guo Wengzhong of Xihe, Lu Wengru in Taiyuan, Er Changqing in Linhuai, and Chen Junru in Dongyang wore the knight's label yet behaved with courteous restraint.
Xihe is a commandery name in the parallel list of each man's place association, not an ordinary directional phrase.
Wang Mang was delighted, recalled Lou Hu to court as former Director of Shining Brightness, enfeoffed him as Marquis of Xixiang, and ranked him among the Nine Ministers.
Wang Mang was delighted, recalled Lou Hu to govern Qianhuiguang Commandery, enfeoffed him as Marquis of Xixiang, and ranked him among the Nine Ministers.
Qianhuiguang was a commandery created by dividing the capital region, not an office called Director of Front Shining Brightness.
Mang was greatly pleased, summoned Hu to serve as former Director of Shining Brightness, enfeoffed him as Marquis of Xixiang, and ranked him among the Nine Ministers.
Mang was greatly pleased, summoned Hu to govern Qianhuiguang Commandery, enfeoffed him as Marquis of Xixiang, and ranked him among the Nine Ministers.
The literal line must also treat Qianhuiguang as the commandery governed by Lou Hu, rather than translating its first graph as former.
During Mang's regency the Huaili rebels Zhao Peng and Huo Hong overran the district under Lou Hu's ministry; he lost his post and became a commoner.
During Mang's regency, the Huaili rebels Zhao Peng and Huo Hong rose in force and spread into Qianhuiguang Commandery; Lou Hu was held responsible, dismissed, and reduced to commoner status.
The jurisdiction is Qianhuiguang Commandery. The revision also restores Lou Hu's responsibility for failing to contain the rebels.

When Mang held the regency, great bandits of Huaili such as Zhao Peng and Huo Hong rose in groups, extending into the former Director of Shining Brightness's jurisdiction; Hu sat guilty and was dismissed to commoner status.

When Mang held the regency, great bandits of Huaili such as Zhao Peng and Huo Hong rose in groups and spread into the territory of Qianhuiguang Commandery; Hu was held responsible, dismissed, and reduced to commoner status.
The literal line must preserve Qianhuiguang as a commandery name and render Lou Hu's resulting official liability.
Chen Zun lost his father young and served with Zhang Song as a Metropolitan clerk.
Orphaned young, Chen Zun served as a clerk in the Metropolitan District alongside Zhang Song, courtesy name Bosong.
The source supplies Zhang Song's courtesy name Bosong, but a parenthetical-style apposition reads more naturally than the worker's insertion.

A provincial inspector once needed an audience at the Secretariat but found Chen Zun mid-orgy; he crawled to Mistress Chen, kowtowed, explained his deadline, and she smuggled him out the back gate while her son reeled.

A provincial inspector once stopped at Chen Zun's residence while on his way to report to the Secretariat, only to find a drinking party in progress. Hard pressed for time, he waited until Zun was thoroughly drunk, forced his way in to see Zun's mother, kowtowed, and explained his deadline. She then had him led out through a rear passage.
The original idiomatic line invents an orgy, crawling, and a woman titled Mistress Chen. The revision follows the stated drinking party and sequence of actions.
Another Chen shared his name; whenever that man announced "Chen Menggong" at a door the room jumped—then groaned when the wrong Chen walked in, so wits dubbed him "Chen Who Frightens the Seats."

Another marquis bore the same surname and courtesy name. Whenever he announced himself at someone's gate as Chen Menggong, everyone within started in excitement, only to be disappointed when the visitor proved not to be Chen Zun. They therefore dubbed him Chen Who Startles the Company.
The source specifies a ranked marquis who shared Chen Zun's surname and courtesy name; the revision removes the ambiguous phrase another Chen shared his name.

Chen Zun's first act in office was to roll a curtain cart into a back lane, join Widow Zuo's singing party, dance on the rafters, collapse drunk among the cushions, and spend the night carried off by her maids.

Soon after taking office, Chen Zun rode a screened carriage into the lanes and called on the widow Zuo Ajun, where wine was served and songs were sung. He rose to dance and caper, collapsed drunk at the gathering, stayed the night, and had her maids help him to bed.
The original drops Zuo Ajun's name and mistakes the idiom 跳梁 for dancing on rafters. The worker restored the name but retained an overly literal beam image.
Shi Dan recommended him for a tough magistracy; at twenty-odd he took Gukou.
Grand Minister of Education Shi Dan recommended him as capable of governing a difficult district, and Yuan She was appointed magistrate of Gukou while still in his twenties.
The proposal correctly restores Shi Dan's office, Yuan She's specific magistracy, and his age; this revision smooths their syntax.
He guarded the empress dowager tomb detail as earth-return colonel.
At Empress Dowager Wenmu's funeral, he served as colonel in charge of the burial works.
Wenmu is the empress dowager's formal Xin title, not an ordinary adjective. The office concerned the earth-restoration work at her burial.
Like Guo Xie he smiled in public and nursed killers within.
Yuan She's nature somewhat resembled Guo Xie's: outwardly warm, benevolent, modest, and yielding, he inwardly concealed a love of killing.
The original invents smiling and employing killers while omitting the explicit outward qualities and Yuan She's own concealed disposition.
Wang Mang hauled him in, scolded his record, then pardoned him and named him both Pacification governor and Grand Administrator of Tianshui.
Wang Mang summoned him, rebuked him for his crimes, then pardoned him and appointed him grand administrator of Zhenrong, Wang Mang's name for Tianshui Commandery.
Zhenrong was Wang Mang's renamed Tianshui Commandery and Dayin his title for its grand administrator, not a second concurrent office.
Wang Mang stranded officials who clung to him lived.
At the time, all of Wang Mang's provincial governors and envoys who attached themselves to Yuan She were spared.
The original sentence is ungrammatical and invents stranded officials. The source says that Mang's officials survived by attaching themselves to Yuan She.
